What he described in the beginning was an Article 15 hearing, also known as "Captain's Mast" or Non-Judicial Punishment (NJP). The "non-judicial" bit is important, because it's exactly that - a non-judicial, non-criminal, administrative procedure. As an aside, a service member facing NJP/Article 15 has the rught under the UCMJ to demand trial by court-martial.

He also mentioned the Judge Advocate General (JAG) as being the militaru lawyers involved in potential tribunals. Half true. In a court-martial, a JAG officer will represent the government prosecution, and another will be assigned to represent the accused. However, the accused does have the right to civilian representation, at their own expense. Dunno if it's different in a "military tribunal." Also, a court-martial is usually an officer serving as judge, sometimes with additional officers (and senior enlisted, if the accused is enlisted) serving as a jury panel.

(Note: he does clarify Art. 15 vs. Court-martial a bit more, but not nearly enough, I think. They are vastly different.)

He is correct that conviction at court-martial is a federal conviction (also a felony conviction), and they can be conducted anywhere US forces are stationed.

Military police, as far as I know, do not have jurisdiction to arrest even US persons on foreign soil unless prior arrangements are made with foreign governments (like SOFA agreements in friendly countries like Japan, where we have a permanent presence). I could be wrong on this point. Regardless, I imagine that will be tricky.
